items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.  PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.  The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.  This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an…

items.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. items.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. items.title: [AINews] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai
items.content: There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “ Weight Space Programming ” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Instead today we’re featuring AI Engineer Shanghai and also sharing an exclusive interview on the history of Latent Space ! AI News for 11/02/2026-11/03/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). Hugging Face reproduction : Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo ( NielsRogge ). Hand-written classifier : A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version ( jacsebl ). Legora's CTO highlighted the result ( mstockton ). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed : GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.content: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the…

items.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → Open video on YouTube ↗ What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not…

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. items.title: Korea’s Stock Market Crashed $1 Trillion. What Does That Mean for the Global AI Race?
items.content: Richard Gray is an analyst who works for a foreign policy think tank in Washington, D.C. Since 2025, South Korea’s capital markets have vacillated from the world’s best-performing to shedding more than $1 trillion in market capitalization. This volatility is a story of how Korea’s financial system overlays supply chain specialization. With Korean firms Samsung and SK hynix controlling a majority share of global memory, South Korea’s stock market functionally operates as a single, highly leveraged node within the AI financial architecture. Two interwoven dynamics explain the convulsions of Korean capital markets and their global ramifications. The first is the Korea discount , in which Korean equities are structurally undervalued because of lagging financial development and weak corporate governance. The second is a memory discount , with each leading high-bandwidth memory (HBM) company (Micron in the U.S., SK hynix and Samsung in Korea) having depressed valuations in their respective markets. The June-July 2026 crash rippled far beyond Korea’s borders and forewarns what may be to come in future market corrections. For Korea, its historically shallow capital markets and exposure to the memory sector — which is now facing emergent Chinese competitors — serve as overlapping pressures on its financial position. In this environment, the threat of a market correction cascading across global markets and the U.S.-China tech competition looms large. The Zenith: Capital Infusion The Korean market is essentially a bet on two companies competing in the same industry. Korea’s memory chip industry has driven exponential year-on-year growth in Korea’s capital markets. From March 2025 to June 2026, the KOSPI — Korea’s main stock index — rose 241%, adding nearly $3.3 trillion in capitalization and exceeding the total increase accumulated over the index’s 43-year history (Bloomberg). items.title: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?
items.content: Zilan Qian is a research scholar at GovAI researching AI development and regulation in China. On October 21, the People’s Daily published a commentary titled “Turning ‘Gunpowder’ into ‘Fireworks’? Beware the Claim That China’s AI Has Gone Astray” (把”火药”做成”烟花”？警惕”中国AI跑偏论”). The same day, Nanfang Commentary (南方评论), the op-ed column of Southern Daily , asked : “Is Half of China’s Compute Being Spent on Feel-Good Dramas (爽剧)? Don’t Judge AI by Its Tokens.” Three days earlier, Beijing News (新京报) had questioned whether “‘American AI Boosts Productivity While Chinese AI Makes Tittytainment’ Is a False Proposition.” All three state-affiliated outlets were responding to the same viral claim: that 55% of China’s AI tokens were being used for short dramas and video generation. The claim struck a nerve because AI-generated entertainment in China is both everywhere and widely despised. According to China’s broadcasting regulator, more than 90% of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. Yet Chinese media and public figures routinely call them wunao (无脑, braindead), cuzhi lanzao (粗制滥造, shoddily made), and zhili dixia (智力低下, intellectually deficient). 1 Why, in a society that places such a premium on productivity, has an industry devoted to manufacturing seemingly useless pleasure become so enormously popular? And what should we make of the shame attached to it? I argue that both answers lie in Chinese society’s obsession with usefulness, where technologies and people alike are judged by their productive value, so much so that resting can feel…

items.title: Xi vs Trump on Corruption
items.content: In February, Eric and Donald Jr. sat down with a reporter to explain why Abu Dhabi paid $500m for a stake in World Liberty Financial. Don Jr. said, “They tried all this nonsense the first time around. Frankly, it’s gotten old…They created this monster.” The monster of political corruption has been with us since the founding. But since the Progressive Eva, it has been cut with at least a tinge of embarrassment. The Trumps instead have done it in broad daylight and tried to make it a flex. China’s political system is riddled with corruption on an entirely different scale. The skims in China happen up and down the system, and making a billion dollars while in office is nothing new for senior Chinese leaders. But Xi understands what this costs the Party. In his first Politburo speech as General Secretary, he warned that corruption, left to spread, would “doom the Party and the state.” Xi was horrified by seeing youth with bloodlines just as red as his crash foreign sports cars in the streets of Beijing. He views the princeling inheritance as a responsibility to serve, not a license to fuckboy. As Kamil Galeev writes , Xi aims to extirpate “the alien, unfamiliar, threatening bandit entrepreneurial culture — not even from the country but rather, from the national elites.” Xi is a believer, but Trump is a businessman. After Trump brought down the guardrails with a compliant SCOTUS and Congress, the presidential family has been sloppily revenue-maximizing ever since. 1 Xi’s anti-corruption campaign hasn’t liquidated corruption in China, which still lubricates a much higher percentage of economic activity than similar behavior does in America. But Xi has succeeded in making it dangerous. selectedItems.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
selectedItems.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.  PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.  The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.  This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an…
